New Mexico.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back only through a governor's pardon, and the pardon must specifically ask for the right to bear arms.
New Mexico.process_note: Apply to the Governor for a pardon to restore civil rights, asking specifically for the right to bear arms; the Parole Board investigates and recommends, and the Governor decides.
New Mexico.waiting_period: 5 to 8 years after discharge from supervision, depending on the felony level (5 years for a 4th-degree felony up to 8 years for a 1st-degree felony), plus one more year to seek the right to bear arms
New Mexico.statute_name: Possession of firearms by a felon
New Mexico.agency_name: Office of the Governor of New Mexico (pardons; New Mexico Parole Board investigates)
New Mexico.state_note: State law bans a person with a felony conviction from having a firearm for 10 years after the sentence ends, and a pardon that does not mention firearms will not restore gun rights.

New York.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back through a Certificate of Relief from Disabilities or a Certificate of Good Conduct, but some convictions are excluded and a handgun still needs a separate license.
New York.process_note: Apply for a Certificate of Relief from Disabilities from the sentencing court, or a Certificate of Good Conduct from the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, and the certificate must specifically state that it restores firearm rights.
New York.waiting_period: none for a Certificate of Relief from Disabilities; 1 to 5 years after release for a Certificate of Good Conduct, depending on the felony level
New York.statute_name: Certificates of Relief from Disabilities and Certificates of Good Conduct
New York.agency_name: New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS), Certificate Review Unit, and the sentencing court
New York.state_note: A certificate must specifically say it restores firearm rights, and Class A-I felonies and violent felonies cannot have the pistol-license bar lifted by a certificate.

North Carolina.restoration_note: A person with a single nonviolent felony conviction can ask a court to restore firearm rights, but violent felonies and people with more than one felony cannot use this route.
North Carolina.process_note: Petition the district court in the county where the person lives, after a hearing where the person must show they meet the law's requirements and are not disqualified.
North Carolina.waiting_period: 20 years after civil rights were restored (when the sentence ended)
North Carolina.agency_name: North Carolina District Court in the county where the person lives
North Carolina.state_note: Only one nonviolent felony qualifies, and Class A, B1, and B2 felonies plus assault, firearm, and sex-offender-registration offenses are excluded.

North Dakota.restoration_note: Firearm rights come back on their own when the ban period ends, and a person with a nonviolent felony can also ask a court to restore them sooner.
North Dakota.process_note: No application is needed once the ban period runs out, but a person with a nonviolent felony may petition the district court for earlier restoration if fines are paid, the sentence is finished, and they are not likely to be a danger to others.
North Dakota.waiting_period: 5 years after conviction or release from prison, parole, or probation for a nonviolent felony, or 10 years for a violent felony, whichever is latest
North Dakota.statute_name: Persons who are not to possess firearms; Restoration of right to possess firearm
North Dakota.state_note: The early court petition is only open to nonviolent felonies, so a person with a violent felony must wait out the full 10-year ban.

Ohio.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can ask a court to lift the firearm ban once the sentence is fully finished.
Ohio.process_note: Apply to the Court of Common Pleas in the county where the person lives for relief from the weapons disability, showing full discharge from prison and supervision and a law-abiding life since then.
Ohio.waiting_period: none — a person may apply any time after being fully discharged from prison, community control, post-release control, and parole
Ohio.agency_name: Court of Common Pleas in the county where the person lives
Ohio.state_note: Relief restores all civil firearm rights, but the court can revoke it, and it is automatically void if the person later commits a violent or drug-trafficking offense.

Oklahoma.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back only through a full pardon, and there is no court petition that restores them.
Oklahoma.process_note: Apply for a pardon through the Pardon and Parole Board, which investigates and holds a hearing; if a majority recommends it, the Governor decides whether to grant the pardon.
Oklahoma.waiting_period: 5 years after being discharged from all sentences and supervision, or after 5 straight years of parole or probation just before applying
Oklahoma.statute_name: Possession of firearms by convicted felons
Oklahoma.agency_name: Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board (recommends; Governor grants)
Oklahoma.state_note: Only a full and complete pardon restores firearm rights in Oklahoma, and a pardon does not erase the conviction from the record.

Oregon.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can ask a court to lift the firearm ban, though Measure 11 offenses and person felonies involving a firearm or deadly weapon are excluded.
Oregon.process_note: File a petition in the circuit court of the county where the person lives, serve a copy on the local police chief or sheriff, and prove by clear and convincing evidence that the person is not a threat to the public or to themselves.
Oregon.waiting_period: 1 year after the felony sentence ends, including parole, probation, and post-prison supervision
Oregon.statute_name: Relief from prohibition against possessing or receiving a firearm
Oregon.agency_name: Oregon Circuit Court in the county where the person lives (Oregon Judicial Department)
Oregon.state_note: Time alone does not restore rights in Oregon — the state Supreme Court has held the 15-year provision does not lift the ban, so a court order, set-aside, or pardon is needed.

Pennsylvania.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back through a governor's pardon, and some people can also ask a court for relief after 10 years.
Pennsylvania.process_note: Apply to the Board of Pardons for clemency; the Board investigates and holds a hearing, and the Governor can only grant a pardon if the Board recommends it.
Pennsylvania.waiting_period: no fixed period for a pardon; 10 years after release from prison for the court-petition route under 18 Pa.C.S. § 6105(d)
Pennsylvania.statute_name: Persons not to possess, use, manufacture, control, sell or transfer firearms
Pennsylvania.state_note: A pardon is the most common route, and the Board of Pardons must recommend it before the Governor can grant it.

Rhode Island.restoration_note: Rhode Island's firearm ban covers crimes of violence rather than every felony, and for a crime of violence there is no court process to restore rights — only a governor's pardon, which is rarely granted.
Rhode Island.process_note: Petition the Governor directly in writing for a pardon, since there is no pardon board or formal application form; the Governor also needs the Senate's consent before granting one.
Rhode Island.waiting_period: no fixed period — a person may petition the Governor at any time, but pardons are rarely granted
Rhode Island.statute_name: Possession of firearms by certain persons prohibited
Rhode Island.agency_name: Office of the Governor of Rhode Island
Rhode Island.state_note: Rhode Island's ban covers crimes of violence, not every felony, so a nonviolent felony alone does not bar firearm possession under state law.

South Carolina.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back only through a pardon, which is granted by a board rather than the Governor.
South Carolina.process_note: Apply to the Department of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services with three letters of support and the fee; the Board of Paroles and Pardons holds a hearing and must approve by at least two-thirds.
South Carolina.waiting_period: none after discharge from a sentence or probation; 5 years under supervision for parolees
South Carolina.statute_name: Guidelines for determining eligibility for pardon
South Carolina.agency_name: South Carolina Department of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services (Board of Paroles and Pardons)
South Carolina.state_note: In South Carolina pardons are granted by a seven-member board, not the Governor, and all restitution must be paid in full before a pardon can be granted.
